paragraphs.text: Honestly the best argument for protecting uninterrupted study time on campus is that focus is what actually makes learning stick. When I get even an hour where nobody is texting me or pulling me into something, I get way more done than in three scattered hours between classes.
Most of us already know this from experience, but the school treats study time like it's optional.
The strongest version of the case isn't just about grades though, it's about how our brains work.

Sustained attention allows the brain to consolidate information into long-term memory, whereas frequent interruptions force a costly re-engagement process that can take upward of twenty minutes to fully recover from. This cognitive switching cost compounds over the course of a day, eroding both productivity and retention.
So if a campus really cares about learning and not just keeping people busy, it makes sense to set aside quiet hours and spaces that don't get scheduled over.

That's the most defensible angle to me because it's hard to argue against actually learning the material. Protecting study time isn't a luxury, it's basically protecting the whole point of being here.
